stories.title: Fashion Boutique Atelier Secures Retail Space at 181 MacDougal Street
stories.excerpt: Fashion boutique Atelier New York is upgrading its retail footprint in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The multi-brand luxury boutique will be the inaugural tenant in the commercial component of the Straus Group’s newly constructed 181 MacDougal Street luxury condominium building, Commercial Observer has learned. Asking rent for the 2,130-square-foot retail space was $250 per square foot, according to landlord broker Newmark. Newmark’s Ariel Schuster, Jackie Totolo and Jordyn Comras negotiated the lease on behalf of the landlord. Atelier did not work with a tenant broker. Atelier’s new storefront sits at the corner of MacDougal and Eighth Street, one block north of Washington Square Park. The retailer was founded along Crosby Street in 2002 as a purveyor of luxury designers’ new and exclusive collections, according to its website. Atelier currently operates two locations near its new 181 MacDougal Street space: a women’s store across the street at 29 West Eighth Street and a men’s store down the block at 20 West Eighth Street. The boutique’s ownership declined to comment on its plans for these locations, including whether it will relocate from either of its existing sites. The retailer estimates the new store at 181 MacDougal Street will open in four to six months. Atelier’s other New York City locations include Tangram Mall in Flushing, Queens, and another nearby Flushing storefront at 138-37 39th Avenue. The retailer also has a location in Seattle. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Atelier boutique leases 2,130 SF at 181 MacDougal, Greenwich Village, $250/SF
Luxury condo retail component achieving initial occupancy; high street rents sustained
Retail demand concentration near Washington Square Park supports mixed-use development
stories.summary: Fashion boutique Atelier New York has signed a lease for 2,130 square feet of retail space at the newly constructed 181 MacDougal Street luxury condominium building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village at $250 per square foot. The space is the inaugural tenant in the commercial component of the Straus Group project and occupies a prime corner location one block north of Washington Square Park. Atelier currently operates two nearby locations, signaling sustained luxury retail demand in the submarket.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. However, strong retail leasing at premium rates ($250/SF) in high-barrier-to-entry Greenwich Village validates mixed-use residential development strategy; luxury condo projects can achieve higher residential pricing when anchored by flagship retail tenants that attract affluent foot traffic. The rapid leasing of inaugural retail space suggests strong asset-class confidence in the Straus Group project and the Village's residential appeal.

stories.title: Fintech Firm Stash Financial Leases 12K SF at 641 Avenue of the Americas
stories.excerpt: This fintech firm is stashing away some new office space. Stash Financial, a digital personal finance and micro-investing company offering financial advice, has inked a 12,322-square-foot office lease at Spear Street Capital’s 641 Avenue of the Americas, Commercial Observer has learned. The lease was signed in mid-August, according to a source close to the deal. The length of the lease was not disclosed, but Stash will occupy space on part of the building’s sixth floor — which spans a total of 22,000 square feet, according to the property’s website. The asking rent was $98 per square foot. The finance firm, which did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment, will move from its current location, a WeWork coworking space at 450 Park Avenue South, the source noted. It is unclear when the move will take place. Jason Greenstein and Jonathan Franzel from Newmark represented the landlord in the deal while CBRE’s Paul Amrich, Neil King, Meghan Allen and Zach Price represented the tenant. Newmark declined to comment, while CBRE did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. Located in Manhattan’s trendy Chelsea neighborhood, 641 Avenue of the Americas is an eight-story Beaux Arts office property located between West 19th and West 20th streets. Other tenants in the building include fragrance company DSM-Firmenich and cloud software company Infor. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Stash Financial exits WeWork, leases 12,322 SF at 641 Ave Americas, $98/SF
Fintech firm consolidating to permanent office; mid-August lease timing reflects Q3 relocation cycle
NYC office market absorbing tech talent relocating from coworking; supply constraint opportunity
stories.summary: Stash Financial, a digital finance and micro-investing company, has leased 12,322 square feet on the sixth floor of 641 Avenue of the Americas in Manhattan at $98 per square foot. The lease, signed in mid-August, represents a move from WeWork's 450 Park Avenue South location. The fintech firm occupies approximately half of the building's 22,000-square-foot floor.
stories.impact: Signals growing maturity and stability of NYC-based fintech; companies exiting coworking for traditional office space typically indicate revenue growth and team expansion. This trend suggests sustained job creation in high-value tech and finance roles in Manhattan, translating to stronger rental demand for Class A residential product targeting young professionals and junior executives in Midtown South and Flatiron submarkets. Recurring pattern of WeWork-to-direct office migration indicates potential for residential demand acceleration in neighborhoods proximate to major office corridors.

stories.title: New Hampshire Rehab Property Trades for $7.5M
stories.excerpt: A former rehab facility in Manchester, NH has changed hands for $7.5 million, with the new owner planning to open a recovery center at the property. Manchester Alcoholism Rehabilitation Center, an affiliate of nonprofit Easterseals, sold the property at 140 Queen City Ave. The buyer is RIO Holdings NH, LLC, an entity linked to the Recovery Institute of Ohio, a substance abuse and mental health treatment center in Sandusky, OH. Colliers represented the buyer while Norton Asset Management and Harrington & Co. represented the seller. The facility previously operated as the Farnum Center, one of the state’s largest inpatient addiction recovery centers. The 70-bed facility ceased inpatient operations in the summer of 2025 due to financial strains. With convenient access to downtown Manchester and Interstate 293, the property’s previous use and existing infrastructure made it especially suitable for RIO’s plans to bring its model of recovery care to New Hampshire. Colliers noted in a statement that the transaction followed a competitive bidding process. The post New Hampshire Rehab Property Trades for $7.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Recovery Institute of Ohio acquires Manchester NH rehab property for $7.5M; specialty-use conversion underway
Farnum Center (70-bed) ceased operations summer 2025 due to financial stress; asset recycled
Healthcare real estate sector experiences use-case shifting; limited multifamily developer relevance
stories.summary: RIO Holdings NH, an entity affiliated with Ohio-based Recovery Institute, has purchased the former Manchester Alcoholism Rehabilitation Center in New Hampshire for $7.5 million. The property, known previously as the Farnum Center, is a 70-bed facility that ceased inpatient operations in summer 2025 due to financial strains. RIO plans to reopen it as a recovery center, leveraging the property's proximity to downtown Manchester and Interstate 293.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily development impact. Specialty healthcare asset conversion does not affect residential supply, demand, or capital flow in Manchester. However, the closure of the Farnum Center and subsequent reactivation signals broader healthcare real estate distress and redeployment cycles; developers tracking regional office-to-residential conversion opportunities in secondary markets should monitor whether any healthcare campuses or underutilized medical office buildings become available for adaptive reuse.

stories.title: Two Roads Settles Biscayne 21 Condo Suit, Paving Way for Edition Condo in Miami
stories.excerpt: Two Roads Development can finally start building its luxury condo development in Miami’s Edgewater neighborhood after reaching a settlement to gain complete control of the waterfront site. The settlement caps a three-year legal stalemate, which had threatened to derail a prominent luxury condo development: the 55-story, Edition-branded high-rise. The Miami-based development firm paid $50 million for the remaining units at the Biscayne 21 condominium building, where the new development will rise, according to a representative for Two Roads Development, who declined to provide additional details about the settlement. Demolition will take place this month, with vertical construction starting soon after. So far, the project is 40 percent sold. “This has been a long and arduous process, and we’re grateful to our team and partners who remained committed throughout,” Taylor Collins, co-founder and managing principal of Two Roads Development, said in a statement. “We’re excited to now turn our full attention to realizing the extraordinary potential of this irreplaceable waterfront site.” The Real Deal first reported news of the settlement. In 2022, Two Roads Development paid at least $150 million for the majority of the units at Biscayne 21, a condominium constructed in 1964 on a 3.5-acre site at 2121 North Bayshore Drive, and launched the 185-unit development with prices starting at $1.7 million. The firm also amended the bylaws of Biscayne 21 to terminate its condo association, a critical move to gain complete control of the 191-unit building to demolish it and eventually begin construction. In response, 10 condo owners, who had not sold their units, sued in 2023. A Florida court sided in favor of the owners, arguing that Two Roads had illegally changed Biscayne 21’s bylaws, a ruling that shocked the South Florida real estate community. The Florida Supreme Court declined to take up Two Roads Development’s appeal in October. Since the deadly collapse of the Champlain Tower
bullets: Two Roads settles Biscayne 21 suit, pays $50M to gain full site control in Miami Edgewater
55-story Edition branded luxury condo; 40% presold; demolition underway; vertical construction imminent
3-year legal cloud cleared; high-barrier waterfront site now unencumbered; luxury condo pipeline accelerates
stories.summary: Two Roads Development has settled a three-year legal stalemate by paying $50 million for remaining units at the Biscayne 21 condominium building, securing complete control of the waterfront site in Miami's Edgewater neighborhood. Demolition is set to begin this month, with vertical construction to follow shortly after. The project, a 55-story Edition-branded luxury residential high-rise, is already 40 percent sold.
stories.impact: Waterfront Miami luxury condo market heating up; high pre-sales absorption (40%) despite extended permitting and legal risk indicates strong demand from affluent buyers in Miami Edgewater submarket. Clearing of title issues removes development friction and opens capital allocation for competing projects; signals that premium waterfront sites in Miami support luxury residential pricing sufficient to justify complex entitlements and litigation costs. Continued Edition brand expansion in Miami reinforces market perception of Edgewater as premier high-rise residential destination, supporting concurrent multifamily rental development opportunities in adjacent submarkets targeting younger professionals priced out of luxury condos.

stories.title: Howard Hughes Inks $35M Refi on Cypress Retail/Office Development
stories.excerpt: Affinius Capital provided a $35 million refinancing for Village Green at Bridgeland Central, a nearly 200,000-square-foot mixed-use retail and office development in Cypress, Texas. Howard Hughes Holdings was the sponsor. The property is in the Bridgeland master-planned community. The 23-acre property is anchored by H-E-B and includes a Class A office building. The property’s office component comprises a three-story, 49,000-square-foot mass-timber building that was nearly fully leased at the time of the loan closing. Bridgeland has 7 million square feet of office space, 2 million square feet of retail space, 3,800 residences, and 1,500 hotel rooms. Colby Mueck, Kelly Layne, Jack Britton and Scot Sarlin of JLL arranged the loan on behalf of Howard Hughes Holdings. The post Howard Hughes Inks $35M Refi on Cypress Retail/Office Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Affinius Capital refi $35M on Village Green Bridgeland Central, Cypress TX; nearly 200K SF mixed-use
HHC-sponsored; H-E-B anchor; 49K SF mass-timber office component nearly fully leased at closing
Master-planned community absorbing significant office and retail; suburban mixed-use capital flowing
stories.summary: Affinius Capital has provided a $35 million refinancing for Village Green at Bridgeland Central, a nearly 200,000-square-foot mixed-use retail and office development in Cypress, Texas, sponsored by Howard Hughes Holdings. The property includes an H-E-B anchor, and its 49,000-square-foot Class A mass-timber office building was nearly fully leased at closing. The 23-acre property is located within the larger Bridgeland master-planned community, which comprises 7 million square feet of office, 2 million square feet of retail, 3,800 residences, and 1,500 hotel rooms.
stories.impact: Bridgeland's scale (7M SF office, 2M SF retail, 3,800+ units) demonstrates successful large-format mixed-use master-planned development model; strong office leasing and refinancing appetite validate suburban Houston office and retail co-location strategy. Multifamily developers should note Bridgeland's ability to absorb 3,800+ residential units at density within master-planned framework; capital flowing to mixed-use components suggests cross-collateral strength and developer optionality. Office leasing momentum in suburban Cypress markets adjacent to major employment clusters; opportunity for complementary build-to-rent or Class A apartments targeting office workers within Bridgeland ecosystem.

stories.title: Bank OZK Lends $76M for Connecticut Office-to-Resi Conversion
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Saber-Hightower and Granoff Real Estate has sealed $75.5 million of construction financing for an office-to-residential conversion project in Connecticut’s Fairfield County, Commercial Observer has learned. Bank OZK provided the loan on the sponsorship’s 286-unit M7 Lofts development in Norwalk, Conn., where two eight-story office buildings now sit within the Merritt 7 Corporate Park. The development team also secured $32 million of JV equity from an undisclosed family office. Greystone Capital Advisors negotiated the transaction with a team consisting of Drew Fletcher, Paul Fried, Bryan Grover and Jesse Kopecky. “This was a compelling adaptive-reuse opportunity that required a financing strategy tailored to the sponsor’s long-term business plan,” Fletcher, president of Greystone Capital Advisors, said in a statement. Located at 101 and 201 Merritt 7, the two buildings slated for conversion are part of the six-building Merritt 7 Corporate Park complex 10 miles northeast of Downtown Stamford, Conn. and less than five-minute walk from the Merritt 7 Metro-North train station. The two buildings will be combined into one apartment complex with amenities that include a fitness center, coworking space and an outdoor pool deck. “These are well-located buildings that can serve Fairfield County far better as housing than as office,” Marty Berger, managing principal of Saber-Hightower, said in a statement. “By leveraging the existing infrastructure at Merritt 7 and the property’s proximity to transit, we can create a differentiated residential experience while giving these buildings a new purpose.” Bank OZK did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Bank OZK funds $75.5M construction on 286-unit M7 Lofts office-to-resi conversion, Norwalk CT
Saber-Hightower and Granoff JV; $32M family office equity; Fairfield County Merritt 7 Corporate Park
Adaptive reuse financing unlocked; office-to-resi conversions gaining lender confidence in secondary markets
stories.summary: A joint venture between Saber-Hightower and Granoff Real Estate has secured $75.5 million in construction financing from Bank OZK for M7 Lofts, a 286-unit office-to-residential conversion in Norwalk, Connecticut. The project converts two eight-story office buildings in Merritt 7 Corporate Park within Fairfield County. The sponsors also raised $32 million in equity from an undisclosed family office. Greystone Capital Advisors negotiated the transaction.
stories.impact: Bank OZK's willingness to provide construction capital for office-to-resi conversions signals lender confidence in adaptive reuse thesis in secondary metros; Fairfield County vacancy and sublease overhang make Class B/C office ripe for conversion. 286-unit conversion unlocks supply in tight Fairfield County submarket while absorbing obsolete office stock. Multifamily developers should evaluate similar office assets in commuter-belt markets (Stamford, Greenwich, New Canaan corridors); family office equity preference for conversion projects suggests strong capital appetite for adaptive reuse deals with longer hold and asset-value-add profiles. Norwalk's proximity to NYC employment suggests rental demand from corporate spillover; conversion model avoids greenfield land risk.

stories.title: Downtown Denver Apartment Building Trades for $110M
stories.excerpt: Carmel Partners bought The Fitzgerald at 1840 Market St. for $110 million. Greystar was the owner and developer of the 282-unit, 11-story building. The mixed-use building with retail spaces on the ground floor opened in 2022. The purchase price equates to about $390,000 per unit. The Denver Business Journal reports that in 2023, Greystar refinanced The Fitzgerald, securing a $99 million loan from Otera Capital. JLL helped arrange that loan. The building includes studios, one- and two-bedroom units with an average size of 963 square feet. Amenities include a fitness studio, coworking spaces, a pool deck and spa and an outdoor social lounge with barbecues and firepits. The post Downtown Denver Apartment Building Trades for $110M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Carmel Partners acquires The Fitzgerald, Denver downtown, 282 units for $110M ($390K/unit)
2022-built mixed-use building; 11 stories; Greystar developer/prior owner; 2023 refi at $99M
Denver class A multifamily trading at premium valuations; strong institutional demand for newer product
stories.summary: Carmel Partners has purchased The Fitzgerald, an 11-story, 282-unit mixed-use apartment building in downtown Denver at 1840 Market Street, for $110 million, or approximately $390,000 per unit. Greystar was the original developer and owner. The building, which opened in 2022 and includes ground-floor retail, was previously refinanced in 2023 by Greystar at $99 million via Otera Capital. Unit mix includes studios, one- and two-bedroom units averaging 963 square feet.
stories.impact: Downtown Denver Class A multifamily commanding strong exit valuations ($390K/unit) despite moderate refinance decline (2023 refi at $99M suggests LTV constraint or market pause); rapid 3-year hold-to-sale cycle by Greystar suggests core-plus strategy success or portfolio rebalancing. Carmel's acquisition at premium pricing validates Denver downtown submarket resilience and sustained investor appetite for newer, mixed-use residential anchors. Multifamily developers should note that Class A products with retail integration in downtown Denver are trading at limited cap rates; ground-lease and retail revenue diversification remain institutional buyer preference. Continued institutional migration to Denver suggests supply tightness in the submarket; future development opportunity if land becomes available near downtown core.

stories.title: Developer Looking to Transform Phoenix Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: One of Phoenix’s oldest shopping centers is gearing up for a potentially major transformation. Camelback Colonnade is 62 years old in its original form, tracing back to the 1964 opening of the East Camelback Mall, or 32 years old since it was redeveloped and dedicated as the Camelback Colonnade in the fall of 1994. Developer Federal Realty Investments is taking advantage of underutilized space at the Camelback Colonnade for a new 216-unit multifamily project, and, based on public filings, there may be more to come. Other uses, such as retail, restaurants and offices, are also in the mix. It’s made its way through planning board review and now has to get the blessing of the Phoenix City Council. Tenants at the Camelback Colonnade include Fry’s Food Stores, Best Buy, Marshalls, PetSmart, Old Navy, Bath & Body Works, Ulta, Michaels, Staples, and Floor & Décor. It also has a Nordstrom Last Chance discount store. The Phoenix Business Journal reports RED Development sold Camelback Colonnade to Federal Realty Investment Trust in 2021 for $162 million. The post Developer Looking to Transform Phoenix Shopping Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Federal Realty Investments planning 216-unit multifamily conversion at Camelback Colonnade, Phoenix
62-year-old center; FRT acquired 2021 for $162M from RED Development; mixed-use redevelopment underway
Enclosed mall adaptive reuse accelerating; retail-to-resi arbitrage unlocking capital in secondary markets
stories.summary: Federal Realty Investment Trust is proposing a 216-unit multifamily project at Camelback Colonnade in Phoenix, utilizing underutilized retail space within the 62-year-old shopping center (originally opened as East Camelback Mall in 1964, redeveloped in 1994). The mixed-use redevelopment also includes retail, restaurant, and office components. FRT acquired the property from RED Development in 2021 for $162 million. The project has passed planning board review and awaits Phoenix City Council approval.
stories.impact: Enclosing mall adaptive reuse gaining momentum in secondary metros; Federal Realty's expertise in real estate investment trust conversion and mixed-use densification makes Camelback Colonnade logical repositioning candidate. 216-unit multifamily component signals arbitrage opportunity between legacy retail valuations and residential conversion economics; FRT's size and institutional capital provide cost-of-capital advantage to execute complex, phased conversions. Phoenix market fundamentals (job growth, in-migration) support rental absorption. Multifamily developers in secondary markets should audit aging retail centers with 10,000+ SF of co-tenanted anchor space; federal real estate investment trust model and increasing lender appetite for mixed-use adaptive reuse reduce project risk. Camelback Colonnade's approval pathway may signal willingness by Phoenix city council to rezone/entitle similar retail-to-resi conversions; monitor for policy precedent and capital flow acceleration.

stories.title: Seafood Restaurant Crab House Takes 7K SF at 11 East 13th Street
stories.excerpt: It’s the catch of the day! All-you-can-eat seafood chain Crab House has secured its fourth New York City location at 11 East 13th Street in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village neighborhood, Commercial Observer has learned. The 6,500-square-foot space between Fifth Avenue and University Place went fishing for a new proprietor in early August, following the departure of Mediterranean tapas restaurant Reyna New York. The lease was signed Friday, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group, with a monthly asking rent of $38,500. Meridian’s Carson Shahrabani and Noam Aziz represented the landlord, Arnold Toren, while KSR’s Ygal Laham negotiated on behalf of Crab House. “It was definitely a competitive lease,” Laham said in a statement to CO. “Crab House has grown well beyond a mom-and-pop operation and is now an established hospitality group, so we were excited to help them secure this location as they continue to expand.” Shahrabani estimated that the previous tenant spent millions on improvements before vacating. The offering included a 3,000-square-foot ground floor and a 3,500-square-foot lower level, both with fully built-out bars. The large space and location just one block southwest of Union Square generated ample interest, and secured its new tenant in just four weeks. “The space was delivered in pristine, turnkey condition,” said Shahrabani. “We conducted nearly 60 walk-throughs, which generated intense competition among almost a dozen prospective offers. It’s amazing to see such strong demand for prime second-generation restaurant space in Manhattan.” Crab House operates two other Manhattan locations, at 218 West 40th Street in Times Square and 135 East 55th Street in Midtown East, as well as a spot in Brooklyn’s Coney Island at 1223 Surf Avenue. Its new location is expected to open its doors in December. Crab House’s ownership could not be immediately reached for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobse
bullets: Crab House signs lease, 6,500 SF, 11 E 13th St, Greenwich Village; $38,500/month ($71/SF annually)
Fourth NYC location; replaced Mediterranean tapas tenant; all-you-can-eat seafood concept expanding
Greenwich Village ground-floor restaurant rents sustained post-pandemic; hospitality tenant replacement tight
stories.summary: All-you-can-eat seafood restaurant Crab House has leased 6,500 square feet at 11 East 13th Street in Manhattan's Greenwich Village between Fifth Avenue and University Place at a monthly asking rent of $38,500 (approximately $71 per square foot annually). The lease was signed Friday and follows the departure of Mediterranean tapas restaurant Reyna New York. This is Crab House's fourth New York City location.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. Ground-floor restaurant leasing in Greenwich Village validates high street retail and hospitality vitality; Crab House expansion (fourth location) signals consumer spending resilience and venue clustering strategy to generate traffic. However, restaurant tenant turnover and replacement cycles do not directly signal demand or capital dynamics for residential developers; notable primarily for confirming that premium Village street-level rents remain supportable by full-service hospitality operators. Monitor if large restaurant/hotel operators begin consolidating or exiting secondary Village submarkets, which would signal weakening tourist and affluent resident spending—a leading indicator of residential rental demand pressure.

stories.title: 18-Story Houston Office Tower Changes Hands
stories.excerpt: Serac Capital Partners, in partnership with National Real Estate Advisors, acquired 3737 Buffalo Speedway in Greenway Plaza. Madison Marquette was the seller. The Houston Business Journal reports 3737 Buffalo Speedway is an 18-story, 390,919-square-foot office tower at the intersection of Buffalo Speedway and Richmond Avenue. Public records show 3737 Buffalo Speedway had an appraised value for tax purposes of $136.3 million as of Jan. 1. The building was designed by Elkus Manfredi and constructed by Harvey-Cleary Builders. The building’s amenities include a conference center, a fitness center and 24-hour security on-site. There also are two on-site restaurants, including Eunice, a modern Cajun-Creole restaurant and raw bar. The building’s tenant roster includes private equity firms, family offices, foundations, law firms and Fortune 100 companies. The Dinerstein Cos. moved into a 34,400-square-foot space on the ninth floor of 3737 Buffalo Speedway. The build-out of the new office is scheduled to be completed by early 2027. The post 18-Story Houston Office Tower Changes Hands appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Serac Capital and NREA acquire 3737 Buffalo Speedway, Houston Greenway Plaza; 18-story, 390K SF office
Madison Marquette seller; tax appraised at $136.3M; Dinerstein Cos. occupying 34.4K SF on 9th floor; completion 2027
Houston office market sees institutional capital recycling; Greenway Plaza remain competitive submarket
stories.summary: Serac Capital Partners, in partnership with National Real Estate Advisors, has acquired 3737 Buffalo Speedway, an 18-story, 390,919-square-foot office tower in Houston's Greenway Plaza, from Madison Marquette. The building, designed by Elkus Manfredi and constructed by Harvey-Cleary Builders, had a tax-appraised value of $136.3 million as of January 1. Tenants include private equity firms, family offices, foundations, law firms, and Fortune 100 companies. The Dinerstein Companies is currently leasing 34,400 square feet on the ninth floor, with build-out completion scheduled for early 2027.
stories.impact: Houston office market experiencing capital recycling through institutional acquirers (Serac, NREA) rather than distressed dispositions; Greenway Plaza's continued tenant stability (Dinerstein expansion through 2027) suggests submarkt resilience despite broader office headwinds. Office-to-multifamily conversion opportunity limited unless tower-specific vacancy accelerates; however, Greenway Plaza's central location and complementary office/corporate demand support adjacent Class A multifamily development. Multifamily developers should monitor office towers in established employment clusters (Greenway, Uptown, Energy Corridor) for potential conversion if ownership cycles accelerate or NOI compression forces strategic repositioning. No immediate supply pressure signal; office capital flow remains intact in core submarkets.
